linear_programming.summary: Spreads a fixed budget of weight over the signals that best predicted the next move in training, strongest first, each up to a cap; the dual simplex method finds the best corner of that budget exactly.
linear_programming.implementationNote: Bridge: HiGHS dual simplex maximises summed IC under a weight budget and per-signal caps; P(up) is a curve fitted on validation. Differs from the spec: It weights this model's causal signals by train-span information coefficients (IC): one instrument alone makes it bang-bang on a sign. Exact given in-sample inputs; shadow prices are logged. Expect: a sparse vertex (top signals at their caps), skill near a one-feature logistic model.

exposure_budget.label: Total weight budget
exposure_budget.description: The absolute signal weights may add up to at most this. Only the mix of weights matters for P(up), because the score is recalibrated on the validation bars.

per_signal_cap.label: Most weight on one signal
per_signal_cap.description: No single signal may carry more absolute weight than this.

information_coefficient_hurdle.label: Information coefficient hurdle
information_coefficient_hurdle.description: A signal's training information coefficient must beat this before it earns weight (the cost of one unit of weight in the program's objective).

native.produces: The optimal continuous weight vector of a linear programme, its objective value and the dual shadow price of every binding constraint, found at a corner of the constraint region.
native.targetVariable: the continuous weight given to each decision variable of the stated linear allocation problem, with the shadow price of each constraint
native.objectiveNote: Both the objective and every constraint are linear, so the best answer sits at a corner of the constraint region and the dual programme's equal optimal value certifies it exactly.

metrics.why: At a finished simplex solve the primal objective equals the dual objective, so the difference between the two is the certificate that the corner returned is the global optimum of the stated weights problem, and a non-zero value means the pivoting stopped early.

The corner is only an allocation if the exposure budget, the per-variable caps and the dual conditions hold to the solver's tolerances, so the largest remaining violation of a row and of its dual, with the termination status, says whether the weights can be used.

A linear objective pushes the whole budget onto the variables with the largest estimated scores, so estimation error is concentrated in exactly the weights it chose; this gap sets the objective value promised at the corner against what those weights earned afterwards.
metrics.baseline: the same weight vector valued on the bars that followed the solve

metrics.why: The optimum is a corner where a few variables sit at their caps and the rest at zero, and a small change in one score can move it to a neighbouring corner, so the share of refits in which each variable stays in the optimal basis shows whether the allocation is stable.

The count of simplex pivots and the remaining reduced-cost infeasibility show how many corners were walked before none improved, which describes the effort of the solve on an ill-scaled constraint matrix and not the worth of the weights.

notApplicable.name: Realized Sharpe Ratio
notApplicable.why: The simplex method returns a corner and its shadow prices and holds no position through time, so a reward-for-risk figure grades the score vector and the engine's trading rule, which is the as-run layer.

notApplicable.name: Annualized Alpha
notApplicable.why: An excess return over a benchmark index needs a traded history and a benchmark, neither of which a walk between corners contains.

notApplicable.name: Maximum Drawdown
notApplicable.why: A drawdown belongs to an equity path through time, and the linear programme is one solve from a fixed score vector.

notApplicable.name: Portfolio Turnover
notApplicable.why: Turnover compares the corners chosen at successive rebalances and so measures how the score vector moves, not the quality of one solve.

notApplicable.name: Calmar Ratio
notApplicable.why: It divides a yearly return by a drawdown, and the optimal corner has neither until something trades it.

notApplicable.name: CVaR (99% Tail Risk)
notApplicable.why: The linear programme has only linear exposure and budget rows and reports no loss distribution from which a tail average could be taken.

notApplicable.name: Logarithmic loss
notApplicable.why: The solver states weights and shadow prices and never odds of an up move, so there is no probability to score until the as-run bridge adds a curve.

notApplicable.name: Validation minus training objective
notApplicable.why: The pivots are steps of a solver toward a fixed optimum and not a learning curve, and the programme's value on later bars is not recorded.

asRun.standInNote: The catalog entry is a solver that allocates capital across instruments and predicts nothing; the runnable model instead spreads a weight budget across this one instrument's feature columns by their training-span information coefficients, strongest first and each up to a cap, reads the weighted sum as a score and turns it into a probability with a validation-fitted curve, so every as-run number measures that information-coefficient scorecard plus its curve and none of them grades the simplex method.
asRun.probabilityNote: The HiGHS dual simplex solve gives each feature column a weight, the bar's score is the weighted sum of its feature values, and the probability of up is a logistic curve with a slope and an intercept applied to that score, fitted by unweighted maximum likelihood on the fold's validation bars only.

stepQuantity.unit: training channel: the negated programme objective, in information coefficient times weight less the hurdle charge on the weight used; validation channel: nats per scored validation bar through a curve fitted on those same validation bars

meaningful.why: The validation curve is monotone, so this number looks through it to the weighted sum itself and tests whether bars scored higher by the capped, budgeted signal weights went up more often; with a negative fitted slope it grades the inverted score.

It is what following the scorecard's call earned after costs under the engine's rule, where the call is long when the weighted sum sits above the cut the validation curve chose, read beside buy and hold on the same folds.
It is the per-bar reward for risk of trading that call with costs, and it depends only on which side of the curve's cut the weighted sum fell and never on how far.
It is the deepest fall of the equity made by trading the call, which shows what happens when the few signals the optimal corner loaded up to their caps stop working on the test bars.
It compares dollars won with dollars lost over the closed trades that the score's crossings of the cut produced, after costs, as a description of the engine's rule applied to this scorecard.
It is the share of closed trades that ended positive, where a trade ends when the weighted sum crosses the curve's cut, a stop or target is hit or the fold ends, so it is read with the trade count.

It is the hit rate of the traded call, which is the weighted sum against a cut the curve placed on validation bars and not against the score's own zero line; it is read beside the majority-class accuracy.
It averages the hit rate on up bars and on down bars, which matters because the curve's intercept can shift the cut until nearly every bar is called the validation majority side.
It sums the four cells of the scorecard-plus-curve calls in one symmetric number that falls to zero when the shifted cut calls a single side on every bar.

It grades the weighted sum after the validation-fitted curve, so it tests scorecard plus curve: the slope and intercept saw the validation bars but never the test bars, and the reference is quoting the fold's training up share.
It is the bounded squared-miss grade of the same scorecard-plus-curve probability and shows how much of the information-coefficient ranking the curve turned into usable odds.

The curve is fitted without class weights, so its output is a frequency claim against the validation base rate, and the binned gap shows whether that mapping of the weighted sum held on the test bars; it is read with the occupied-bin count.
It shows without bins whether the stretch the curve learned for the weighted sum on validation bars is still the right stretch on the test bars.

The simplex optimum is a corner that can leave only a handful of signals at their caps, so the count of different probability values per fold shows whether the ranking number rests on a real spread of scores or on a few steps.

The forecast line is the same weighted sum multiplied by one slope fitted through the origin on the training bars, so this tests whether that rescaled scorecard beats forecasting no move on the same resolved bars after tick rounding.
It is the typical miss in points of the rescaled scorecard after tick rounding, read beside the no-change forecast's error on the same bars.

It is how often the sign of the rescaled weighted sum matched the actual move where both are non-zero after tick rounding, which grades the score's own zero line with the training-fitted orientation and no validation curve.

The forecast takes its sign from the weighted sum and a training-fitted slope while the traded call takes it from the validation curve, so this share shows how often the curve's shifted or inverted cut overruled the scorecard's own sign.
It shows how often the call came out long, which exposes a fold where the curve's intercept pushed the cut past almost every weighted sum.
It counts how often the weighted sum crossed the curve's cut or a trade otherwise ended, which is needed to read every trading number of this scorecard.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: Neither the linear programme nor the unweighted validation curve uses class weights, so the half-and-half score matches no stage of this model.
With long_only off and no stop or target the engine is always long or short once the first call is made, so the share of bars in a position describes the engine's rule and not the solved weights.

The training channel holds the negated programme objective in information-coefficient units and the validation channel holds a logarithmic loss in nats, so their difference compares two different quantities.
It is the selection score that picked the per-signal cap and the information coefficient hurdle inside the training span, optimistic by construction and not a result of the solved weights.

caveats: The slope and intercept of the logistic curve are fitted on the validation bars, so the validation loss shown for the solver pass is in sample for those two numbers and only the test walk is out of sample.
If the fitted slope is negative the curve inverts the weighted sum, so the traded call can be the opposite of the direction the scorecard's weights point to.

The information coefficients are measured on the same training bars the programme then optimises over, so the objective value the simplex method proves optimal is an in-sample promise and the proof covers the arithmetic, not the forecast.

The optimal corner can put the whole budget on a small number of signals, so the score may take few distinct levels on a fold when those feature columns do, and a ranking measure on few levels is a curve of few points.
The price line is the same weighted sum times one training-fitted slope, so the forecast metrics and the direction metrics grade one set of weights through two different readouts.
Consecutive scored bars share future bars because the label horizon overlaps, so any interval around these numbers needs a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance and never a binomial interval.
On roots other than the Micro Nasdaq future the cost per side is the Micro Nasdaq account figure applied as a stated assumption.
The last bar of each fold exits at its close while every other exit fills at the next bar's open.

mixed_integer_programming.summary: Chooses at most a handful of signals that do not repeat each other, and how much weight each gets, in one exact solve: yes/no switches for the choice, continuous weights for the size.
mixed_integer_programming.implementationNote: Bridge: HiGHS branch and cut picks at most K signals (binary switches) and their weights, no two correlated above a limit; P(up) is a curve fitted on validation. Differs from the spec: It weights this model's causal signals by train-span information coefficients (IC): one instrument alone makes it bang-bang on a sign. In-sample selection is optimistic. The solve stops at the relative gap tolerance or the node limit, so a status other than optimal means the selection is the best found and the logged gap says how far the proof got.
The price line is the same weighted sum of the selected signals times one training-fitted slope, so the forecast metrics and the direction metrics grade one selection through two different readouts.
Consecutive scored bars share future bars because the label horizon overlaps, so any interval around these numbers needs a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance and never a binomial interval.
On roots other than the Micro Nasdaq future the cost per side is the Micro Nasdaq account figure applied as a stated assumption.
The last bar of each fold exits at its close while every other exit fills at the next bar's open.

quadratic_programming.summary: Builds a mean-variance portfolio of signals: rewards each signal's training edge and charges for the risk of signals that win and lose together, like a Markowitz portfolio of strategies.
quadratic_programming.implementationNote: Bridge: OSQP solves Markowitz over signals: IC as return, Ledoit-Wolf covariance of their profit streams as risk; P(up) is a curve fitted on validation. Differs from the spec: It weights this model's causal signals by train-span information coefficients (IC): one instrument alone makes it bang-bang on a sign. Exact given in-sample inputs. Expect: smooth, diversified weights, close to ridge regression.

risk_aversion.label: Risk aversion
risk_aversion.description: How much the program pays for the variance of the combined signal book; higher spreads weight across signals that do not move together.

exposure_budget.label: Total weight budget
exposure_budget.description: The absolute signal weights may add up to at most this. Only the mix of weights matters for P(up), because the score is recalibrated on the validation bars.

per_signal_cap.label: Most weight on one signal
per_signal_cap.description: No single signal may carry more absolute weight than this.

solver_tolerance.label: Solver tolerance
solver_tolerance.description: OSQP's absolute and relative residual tolerance before polishing.

native.produces: The optimal continuous weight vector of a convex quadratic programme, the variance and expected return it reaches and the dual price of every binding constraint.
native.targetVariable: the continuous weight given to each decision variable when estimated return is traded against estimated variance under linear budget and exposure rows
native.objectiveNote: The objective adds a variance term built from an estimated covariance matrix to the linear return term, with one risk-aversion number setting the exchange rate between them, so the answer is a point on the efficient frontier and not a corner.

metrics.why: A convex quadratic programme has a dual whose value meets the primal at the optimum, so the remaining difference between the two certifies how close the returned weights are to the best risk-and-return trade the stated covariance and return estimates allow.

The weights are an optimum only when the stationarity, budget and bound conditions all hold together, so the largest remaining violation of a constraint and of its dual condition, with the termination status, shows whether the solver stopped at the frontier point or merely near it.

Mean-variance weights lean hardest on the assets whose return was overestimated and whose variance was underestimated, so the risk-adjusted value the solve promises is optimistic; this gap sets the promised return less risk charge against what the same weights delivered afterwards.
metrics.baseline: the same weight vector valued on the bars that followed the solve

metrics.why: A covariance matrix estimated from a short trailing window is noisy and can swing the weights from one rebalance to the next, so the share of refits in which each variable keeps a non-zero weight and each bound stays binding shows how much shrinkage is still needed.

The count of active-set changes or barrier iterations and the final residual of the optimality system describe the effort of the solve on a nearly singular covariance matrix, which is a property of the numerics and not of the portfolio.

notApplicable.name: Realized Sharpe Ratio
notApplicable.why: The quadratic solve trades estimated return against estimated variance once and holds no position through time, so a realised reward-for-risk figure grades the estimates and the engine's trading rule, which is the as-run layer.

notApplicable.name: Annualized Alpha
notApplicable.why: An excess return over a benchmark index needs a traded history and a benchmark, neither of which a single mean-variance solve contains.

notApplicable.name: Maximum Drawdown
notApplicable.why: A drawdown belongs to an equity path through time, and the quadratic programme penalises variance at one rebalance with no path.

notApplicable.name: Portfolio Turnover
notApplicable.why: Turnover compares the weights of successive rebalances and so measures how the estimates move, and the programme described carries no turnover term.

notApplicable.name: Calmar Ratio
notApplicable.why: It divides a yearly return by a drawdown, and the frontier point has neither until something trades it.

notApplicable.name: CVaR (99% Tail Risk)
notApplicable.why: The quadratic programme measures risk by variance alone and reports no loss distribution from which a tail average could be taken.

notApplicable.name: Logarithmic loss
notApplicable.why: The solver states weights and dual prices and never odds of an up move, so there is no probability to score until the as-run bridge adds a curve.

notApplicable.name: Validation minus training objective
notApplicable.why: The iterations are steps of a solver toward a fixed optimum and not a learning curve, and the programme's value on later bars is not recorded.

asRun.standInNote: The catalog entry is a solver that builds a mean-variance portfolio across instruments and predicts nothing; the runnable model instead builds a mean-variance book across this one instrument's feature columns, with each signal's training-span information coefficient as its return and the shrunk covariance of the signals' profit streams as its risk, reads the weighted sum as a score and turns it into a probability with a validation-fitted curve, so every as-run number measures that book of signals plus its curve and none of them grades the quadratic solver.
asRun.probabilityNote: The OSQP solve gives each feature column a mean-variance weight, the bar's score is the weighted sum of its feature values, and the probability of up is a logistic curve with a slope and an intercept applied to that score, fitted by unweighted maximum likelihood on the fold's validation bars only.

stepQuantity.unit: training channel: the negated programme objective, the book's summed information coefficient less half the risk-aversion-weighted variance of the signals' profit streams; validation channel: nats per scored validation bar through a curve fitted on those same validation bars

meaningful.why: The validation curve is monotone, so this number looks through it to the mean-variance weighted sum and tests whether bars scored higher by the diversified book of signals went up more often; with a negative fitted slope it grades the inverted score.

It is what following the signal book's call earned after costs under the engine's rule, where the call is long when the mean-variance weighted sum sits above the cut the validation curve chose, read beside buy and hold on the same folds.

It is the realised per-bar reward for risk of trading the call with costs, which is a different thing from the in-sample return-for-variance trade the programme optimised: it depends only on which side of the curve's cut the weighted sum fell.

It is the deepest fall of the equity made by trading the call, which shows whether charging for signals that win and lose together really produced a book that does not fail all at once on the test bars.
It compares dollars won with dollars lost over the closed trades that the score's crossings of the cut produced, after costs, as a description of the engine's rule applied to this book of signals.

It is the share of closed trades that ended positive, where a trade ends when the mean-variance weighted sum crosses the curve's cut, a stop or target is hit or the fold ends, so it is read with the trade count.

It is the hit rate of the traded call, which is the mean-variance weighted sum against a cut the curve placed on validation bars and not against the book's own zero line; it is read beside the majority-class accuracy.
It averages the hit rate on up bars and on down bars, which matters because the curve's intercept can shift the cut until nearly every bar is called the validation majority side.
It sums the four cells of the signal-book-plus-curve calls in one symmetric number that falls to zero when the shifted cut calls a single side on every bar.

It grades the mean-variance weighted sum after the validation-fitted curve, so it tests signal book plus curve: the slope and intercept saw the validation bars but never the test bars, and the reference is quoting the fold's training up share.
It is the bounded squared-miss grade of the same book-plus-curve probability and shows how much of the diversified ranking the curve turned into usable odds.

The curve is fitted without class weights, so its output is a frequency claim against the validation base rate, and the binned gap shows whether that mapping of the book's weighted sum held on the test bars; it is read with the occupied-bin count.
It shows without bins whether the stretch the curve learned for the mean-variance weighted sum on validation bars is still the right stretch on the test bars.

The forecast line is the same mean-variance weighted sum multiplied by one slope fitted through the origin on the training bars, so this tests whether that rescaled book beats forecasting no move on the same resolved bars after tick rounding.
It is the typical miss in points of the rescaled signal book after tick rounding, read beside the no-change forecast's error on the same bars.

It is how often the sign of the rescaled mean-variance sum matched the actual move where both are non-zero after tick rounding, which grades the book's own zero line with the training-fitted orientation and no validation curve.

The forecast takes its sign from the mean-variance sum and a training-fitted slope while the traded call takes it from the validation curve, so this share shows how often the curve's shifted or inverted cut overruled the book's own sign.
It shows how often the call came out long, which exposes a fold where the curve's intercept pushed the cut past almost every value of the book's weighted sum.
It counts how often the mean-variance weighted sum crossed the curve's cut or a trade otherwise ended, which is needed to read every trading number of this book of signals.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: Neither the quadratic programme nor the unweighted validation curve uses class weights, so the half-and-half score matches no stage of this model.
With long_only off and no stop or target the engine is always long or short once the first call is made, so the share of bars in a position describes the engine's rule and not the solved book.
The training channel holds the negated mean-variance objective of the signal book and the validation channel holds a logarithmic loss in nats, so their difference compares two different quantities.
It is the selection score that picked the risk aversion inside the training span, optimistic by construction and not a result of the solved weights.

caveats: The slope and intercept of the logistic curve are fitted on the validation bars, so the validation loss shown for the solver pass is in sample for those two numbers and only the test walk is out of sample.
If the fitted slope is negative the curve inverts the weighted sum, so the traded call can be the opposite of the direction the signal book points to.

The information coefficients and the covariance of the profit streams are measured on the same training bars the programme then optimises over, so the return-for-variance value at the optimum is an in-sample promise.

OSQP is an operator-splitting solver stopped at the solver tolerance with its polishing step switched off, so the weights are optimal to that tolerance and not exactly, and weights near a cap can sit slightly off it.

The risk the programme charges is the variance of the signals' profit streams, which is not the risk of the single position the engine trades, so the solved trade-off and the realised drawdown describe different things.
The price line is the same mean-variance weighted sum times one training-fitted slope, so the forecast metrics and the direction metrics grade one set of weights through two different readouts.
Consecutive scored bars share future bars because the label horizon overlaps, so any interval around these numbers needs a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance and never a binomial interval.
On roots other than the Micro Nasdaq future the cost per side is the Micro Nasdaq account figure applied as a stated assumption.
The last bar of each fold exits at its close while every other exit fills at the next bar's open.

interior_point_method.summary: Fits a sparse logistic regression (L1 penalty) with a primal-dual interior-point solver, the method's classic use in machine learning, and proves how close it got with a duality-gap certificate.
interior_point_method.implementationNote: Bridge: CLARABEL's primal-dual barrier method fits L1 logistic regression (Huber for the price); P(up) is the model's own sigmoid. Differs from the spec: the spec is a solver; predictions match any exact L1 logistic solver. Only the algorithm and its duality-gap certificate differ. Expect: logistic-regression skill with fewer non-zero weights.

l1_penalty.label: L1 penalty
l1_penalty.description: How hard the absolute weights are penalised; larger zeroes more signals.

iteration_count.label: Most Newton iterations
iteration_count.description: The barrier method stops after this many Newton steps.

duality_gap_tolerance.label: Duality gap tolerance
duality_gap_tolerance.description: The solver is done when the gap between the primal and dual objectives is below this.

step_fraction_to_boundary.label: Step fraction to the boundary
step_fraction_to_boundary.description: Each Newton step goes at most this fraction of the way to the edge of the feasible cone.

maximum_training_bars.label: Most recent training bars used
maximum_training_bars.description: The fit uses at most this many of the latest training bars (0 = all); the conic program grows with every bar.

native.produces: The primal solution of a linear or convex quadratic programme, its dual multipliers and the achieved duality gap, reached by following the central path through the inside of the feasible region.
native.targetVariable: the value of each decision variable of the stated linear or convex quadratic allocation programme, with the dual multiplier of each constraint
native.objectiveNote: The method adds a logarithmic barrier that keeps every iterate strictly inside the constraints and shrinks its weight toward zero, so the programme it finally solves is the stated one and the barrier is only the road to it.

metrics.why: Every barrier iterate carries a primal value and a dual value, and their difference, the duality gap, shrinks with the barrier weight, so this number is the method's own certificate of how far the returned point can still be from the true optimum when the iteration limit or tolerance stops it.
metrics.baseline: the duality gap tolerance the same solve was asked to reach

metrics.why: An infeasible-start barrier solve drives the primal and dual feasibility errors to zero alongside the gap, so the largest remaining violation of a constraint and of its dual, with the termination status, shows whether the central path really arrived inside the allowed region.

The count of Newton steps on the linearised optimality system and the remaining complementarity between variables and slacks show how the path-following went on an ill-conditioned constraint matrix, which is the method's practical failure mode and not a grade of the allocation.

The cost vector and constraint data are estimated from past bars, so the objective value the barrier solve reports for its own point is a promise made in sample; this gap sets it against what the same point delivered on the bars after the solve.
metrics.baseline: the same solution valued on the bars that followed the solve

notApplicable.name: Realized Sharpe Ratio
notApplicable.why: The barrier method returns a point and a duality gap and holds no position through time, so a reward-for-risk figure grades the estimates fed into the programme and the engine's trading rule, which is the as-run layer.

notApplicable.name: Annualized Alpha
notApplicable.why: An excess return over a benchmark index needs a traded history and a benchmark, neither of which a sequence of Newton steps contains.

notApplicable.name: Maximum Drawdown
notApplicable.why: A drawdown belongs to an equity path through time, and the barrier solve ends at one point for one set of problem data.

notApplicable.name: Portfolio Turnover
notApplicable.why: Turnover compares successive solutions and so measures how the problem data move between rebalances, not how well one central path was followed.

notApplicable.name: Calmar Ratio
notApplicable.why: It divides a yearly return by a drawdown, and the solver's returned point has neither until something trades it.

notApplicable.name: CVaR (99% Tail Risk)
notApplicable.why: A tail-loss measure describes a distribution of outcomes, and the barrier method reports only the optimum of the programme it was handed.

notApplicable.name: Logarithmic loss
notApplicable.why: Natively the method solves a programme and states no odds of an up move; a probability appears only as run, where the programme it is handed happens to be a logistic regression.

notApplicable.name: Validation minus training objective
notApplicable.why: The Newton iterations are steps of a solver toward a fixed optimum and not a learning curve, and the programme's value on later bars is not recorded.

asRun.standInNote: The catalog entry describes a barrier solver for allocation programmes and has no prediction of its own; the runnable model hands that kind of solver, CLARABEL's primal-dual barrier method, a sparse logistic regression with an absolute-value penalty on the weights, so the as-run numbers measure that logistic regression, which any exact solver of the same problem would reproduce, and only the logged duality-gap certificate speaks about the barrier method itself.
asRun.probabilityNote: CLARABEL's primal-dual barrier method minimises the unweighted logistic loss plus an absolute-value penalty on the weights over the most recent maximum_training_bars labelled training bars, and the probability of up is the sigmoid of that fitted weighted sum plus its intercept with no validation curve on top.

stepQuantity.unit: training channel: nats per training bar plus the absolute-value penalty on the weights; validation channel: nats per scored validation bar with no penalty

meaningful.why: The barrier solve minimises exactly this quantity on the training bars, apart from the penalty that zeroes weak weights, and nothing is selected on validation, so on the test bars it is the honest out-of-sample value of the model's own objective, read against quoting the fold's training up share.
It tests whether the sparse weighted sum the penalty left standing orders the bars, so that bars with a higher sum went up more often, independent of whether the sigmoid's scale is right.
It is the bounded squared-miss grade of the sigmoid of the penalised weighted sum, a second proper score that a few confidently wrong bars cannot dominate.

The absolute-value penalty shrinks the weights toward zero, which tends to make the stated odds too timid, and a slope away from one on the test bars shows that shrinkage or an overfit in the other direction without using bins.

The logistic loss is unweighted and the intercept is free, so the sigmoid's output is a frequency claim against the training base rate and the binned gap shows whether it held on the test bars; it is read with the occupied-bin count.
A penalty strong enough to zero every weight leaves only the intercept, and every bar then gets the training up share, which this spread of the stated probabilities shows directly.

It is the hit rate of the traded call, which is long when the penalised weighted sum plus intercept is at or above zero, read beside the majority-class accuracy because the free intercept carries the training base rate.
It averages the hit rate on up bars and on down bars, which shows whether the sparse weights separate the two sides or the intercept alone calls the training majority side.
It sums the four cells of the sparse logistic calls in one symmetric number that falls to zero when the intercept dominates and one side is called on every bar.

It is what following the sign of the sparse logistic regression's call earned after costs under the engine's rule of following the latest call and filling at the next bar's open, read beside buy and hold on the same folds.
It is the per-bar reward for risk of trading that call with costs, and it depends only on which side of one half the sigmoid fell and never on how confident it was.
It is the deepest fall of the equity made by trading the call, which shows the cost of weights fitted on only the most recent training bars when the test bars move away from them.
It compares dollars won with dollars lost over the closed trades that the call's flips produced, after costs, as a description of the engine's rule applied to the sparse logistic calls.
It is the share of closed trades that ended positive, where a trade ends when the sigmoid crosses one half, a stop or target is hit or the fold ends, so it is read with the trade count.

It grades a second barrier solve, a Huber-loss regression with the same absolute-value penalty fitted to the scaled move, against forecasting no move on the same resolved bars; it shares the solver and the penalty but none of the classifier's weights.
It is the typical miss in points of the separately solved Huber regression after tick rounding, read beside the no-change forecast's error on the same bars.

It is how often the sign of the Huber regression's forecast matched the actual move where both are non-zero after tick rounding; it can disagree with the traded call, which comes from the logistic solve.
It shows how often the call came out long, which exposes a fold where the penalty left so little weight that the intercept decided nearly every bar.
It counts how often the sigmoid crossed one half or a trade otherwise ended, which is needed to read every trading number of this sparse logistic model.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: The logistic loss handed to the barrier solver carries no class weights, so the output tracks the training base rate and the half-and-half score grades a prior this model never targeted.
With long_only off and no stop or target the engine is always long or short once the first call is made, so the share of bars in a position describes the engine's rule and not the fitted weights.
The training channel adds the absolute-value penalty on the weights to the logistic loss and the validation channel does not, so their difference mixes overfit with the size of the penalty term.
It is the selection score that picked the penalty strength inside the training span, optimistic by construction and not a result of the fitted weights.

caveats: The duality-gap certificate logged after the solve bounds how far the weights are from the exact optimum of the penalised training loss; it certifies the arithmetic of the fit and says nothing about skill on later bars.
The fit uses at most the latest maximum_training_bars labelled training bars, so older training bars in the fold never touch the weights.
The price line is a second model, a Huber regression with the same penalty solved separately, so the forecast metrics and the direction metrics grade two different fits.
Consecutive scored bars share future bars because the label horizon overlaps, so any interval around these numbers needs a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance and never a binomial interval.
On roots other than the Micro Nasdaq future the cost per side is the Micro Nasdaq account figure applied as a stated assumption.
The last bar of each fold exits at its close while every other exit fills at the next bar's open.

convex_optimization.summary: Finds the book of signals with the smallest average loss on its worst bars (conditional value at risk) among those that still earn a required training edge; the program is checked convex and solved exactly.
convex_optimization.implementationNote: Bridge: CLARABEL solves a DCP-checked program: least conditional value at risk of training losses for a required IC edge, plus elastic net. P(up) is a curve fitted on validation. Differs from the spec: It weights this model's causal signals by train-span information coefficients (IC): one instrument alone makes it bang-bang on a sign. Tail bars are thinned evenly to a cap. Expect: weights tilted away from fat-tailed signals, skill near the QP.

tail_confidence_level.label: Tail confidence level
tail_confidence_level.description: Conditional value at risk averages the losses beyond this quantile of the training bars.

required_edge_fraction.label: Required edge (share of the most)
required_edge_fraction.description: The book must earn at least this share of the largest training edge the budget can buy (all of it on the strongest signal); higher trades tail safety for edge.

elastic_net_strength.label: Elastic net strength
elastic_net_strength.description: The overall size of the weight penalty.

elastic_net_mixing.label: Elastic net mixing
elastic_net_mixing.description: 1 = all absolute-value (L1) penalty, 0 = all squared (L2) penalty.

exposure_budget.label: Total weight budget
exposure_budget.description: The absolute signal weights may add up to at most this. Only the mix of weights matters for P(up), because the score is recalibrated on the validation bars.

maximum_scenario_rows.label: Most tail scenario bars
maximum_scenario_rows.description: The tail is measured on at most this many training bars, spread evenly over the span; each adds one variable to the program.

native.produces: The optimal decision vector of a convex programme, its objective value, and dual variables that certify the optimum and price each constraint.
native.targetVariable: The decision vector (for example signal or position weights) that minimises a stated convex cost, risk or negative-return criterion inside a convex feasible region; it is not a statement about the next price move.
native.objectiveNote: Convexity adds the promise that any point with no improving direction is the global best, so a single solve carries a duality-gap certificate and needs no restarts.

metrics.why: Strong duality is the whole reason to pose the problem as convex, so the distance between the returned objective and the dual value is the direct measure of whether the solver delivered the certified global optimum.
metrics.baseline: The duality-gap tolerance the solver was asked to reach.

metrics.why: The Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions need the returned weights to sit inside the budget and inequality constraints and the dual prices to be valid, so the largest primal and dual violation says whether the reported optimum is an answer at all.
metrics.baseline: The feasibility tolerance the solver was asked to reach.

metrics.why: The interior-point or first-order iteration count and the last change between iterates show what the certificate cost and whether the solve stopped on tolerance or on its iteration limit.

The programme is exact only for the trailing-window data it was given, so the objective value it certified minus the value the same weights earn on later bars measures how much of the optimum was fitted estimation noise.
metrics.baseline: Zero, which would mean the certified in-sample objective was honest about later bars.

metrics.why: The specification names the problem data as the only generalisation risk of a convex programme, so how much of the chosen weights, or of the set of constraints that bind, reappears when the programme is refitted on each new trailing window shows whether the solved allocation is knowledge or window noise.

notApplicable.name: Realized Sharpe Ratio
notApplicable.why: It measures a trading rule and its costs over time, which exist only once the Model Cycle trades the solved weights; natively the solver is graded by its certificate.

notApplicable.name: Annualized Alpha
notApplicable.why: No benchmark and no return stream exist in a convex solve, and the metric registry carries no alpha measure.

notApplicable.name: Maximum Drawdown
notApplicable.why: It describes an equity path over many bars, while the native result is a single optimal decision vector.

notApplicable.name: Portfolio Turnover
notApplicable.why: Turnover is at most a penalty term inside the programme's objective and never a measure of solution quality.

notApplicable.name: Calmar Ratio
notApplicable.why: It needs annualised profit and a drawdown, neither of which a solver produces before its answer is traded.

notApplicable.name: CVaR (99% Tail Risk)
notApplicable.why: Tail risk can be what the programme minimises, yet as a score of the method it says nothing about whether the optimum was reached and certified.

notApplicable.name: Kept solution's objective on validation minus on training
notApplicable.why: The solver has no learning curve and no validation value of its programme, so there is no pair of like quantities to subtract.

asRun.standInNote: The specification is a general convex solver; the runnable adapter poses one particular programme, the book of this instrument's feature signals with the least conditional value at risk of training losses that still earns a required information-coefficient edge, with an elastic-net charge, and then bends the book's score into a probability with a logistic curve fitted on validation bars, so every as-run number measures that programme's weights plus that curve.
asRun.probabilityNote: The score of a bar is the solved weights times its feature row, and the probability of up is a logistic curve of that score whose slope and intercept are fitted by unweighted maximum likelihood on the fold's validation bars only.

stepQuantity.unit: the training value is the minimised conditional value at risk plus the elastic-net charge (dimensionless) and the validation value is in nats per bar, one value for the single solver pass

meaningful.why: The logistic curve is monotone, so the ordering of bars is the tail-risk-minimising book's own ordering and this number tests whether that weighted score separates up bars from down bars.
It grades the stated odds of the book's score after the validation-fitted curve on test bars the curve never saw, and nothing was selected on it because the single solve keeps no checkpoint.
A bounded second view of the same book-plus-curve probability, useful because a weak score makes the curve hover near one half where the logarithmic loss barely moves.
It checks whether the slope and intercept learned on the validation bars still describe the book's score on the later test bars; few bins are filled when the curve is flat.
A book whose score carries no information gets a near-zero slope from the curve, which shows up here as a probability that never leaves the validation up share.

It is what trading the sign of the curve's output earned after costs, which tests the tail-averse book's direction call under the engine's rule and not the conditional value at risk the programme minimised.
The same series held long is the reference that shows whether the book's flips between long and short added anything beyond the drift of the folds.
It tests the steadiness of the per-bar profit of the book's call under the engine's rule and costs; the programme controlled the tail of training losses of the signals, not this ratio.

The programme was built to keep the worst training bars small, so the deepest fall of the traded equity is the nearest out-of-sample look at whether that tail aversion carried into the direction call.
It compares the winning and losing trades produced by the flips of the book's call, read beside the trade count because a flat curve makes few flips.
It counts how often a trade opened on the book's call closed in profit after costs, a property of the call and the engine's exits together.
It scores the hard call made by cutting the curve at one half, which depends on the intercept fitted on validation bars as much as on the book's weights.
It shows whether the book-plus-curve call finds both up and down bars or simply leans to the side the validation intercept favoured.
One symmetric number for the cut of the curve at one half, which stays near zero when the fitted intercept makes the book call nearly every bar the same way.
The forecast is the book's score times one least-squares slope from the training span, so this tests whether the size of the score tracks the size of the move better than forecasting no move.
It is the miss in points of the rescaled book score, read against the no-change error on the same bars because the readout has a single free slope.
The sign of the forecast is the sign of the raw book score times its training slope, so this shows the book's direction before the validation curve shifts or inverts it.
It counts how often the raw sign of the book's score matches the traded call, and a low share means the validation curve's intercept or a negative slope overrode the programme.

The logged edge the returned book reached, set against the edge the programme required, shows whether the book meets its one logged constraint; the exposure budget and the rule that a signal is traded only in the direction of its information coefficient are not logged as a residual.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: The training value is the programme's tail-risk objective and the validation value is a logarithmic loss, so the difference compares two unrelated quantities.
With long only off and no stop or target the engine is always in the market once the first call is made, so the share describes the engine's rule and not the book.
Its reference is the test bars' own up share, known only in hindsight, so it cannot be used as a same-model reference for the book-plus-curve probability.

The adapter logs only the solver status, the conditional value at risk reached, the edge reached, the dual price of the edge requirement and the iteration count, so no gap is recorded for this programme.

The single solver pass logs one training value, the minimised conditional value at risk plus the elastic-net charge, beside a validation logarithmic loss; there is no learning curve and nothing is selected on validation.
The scenario bars of the tail-risk programme are the training bars thinned evenly to the maximum scenario rows parameter, so the tail is estimated from a subsample when the training span is long.

The hyperparameter search scores each trial by the traded Sharpe ratio on inner blocks of the training span, which is not the programme's own objective.

asRun.standInNote: The specification is a general exact search framework with no predictor in it, so the runnable adapter gives it one concrete problem: a leaps-and-bounds tree search for the subset of exactly maximum_selected_signals feature columns whose least-squares fit of the standardised forward move has the smallest residual sum of squares on the training span; the as-run numbers therefore measure that best-subset regression score read through a validation-fitted probability curve, not the search framework.
asRun.probabilityNote: The score of a bar is the chosen subset's least-squares coefficients times its feature values, and the probability of up is a two-parameter logistic curve of that score fitted by unweighted maximum likelihood on the fold's validation rows.

stepQuantity.unit: training channel: residual sum of squares of the standardised move for the incumbent subset; validation channel: nats

meaningful.why: The tree search minimised squared error of the forward move, so the forecast, which is the incumbent subset's score rescaled by one training-span slope, is the most direct out-of-sample test of what was certified.

The incumbent subset's fitted value is a continuous score, and this ranking number tests whether larger fitted moves precede up bars while depending on the validation curve only through the sign of its slope.
It reports what trading the sign of the calibrated best-subset score earned after costs, a consequence the least-squares objective never considered because it knows nothing of fills or fees.
It expresses the same test-walk result of the incumbent subset's calls per unit of bar-to-bar variation, for comparing versions of this model with different values of maximum_selected_signals.
A subset proven best on the training span is also the most tightly fitted one, and the deepest fall of the test equity shows what that tight fit cost when the relationships shifted.
It sets summed winning trades against summed losing trades from the incumbent subset's calls, describing how the net result was built and not something the search bounded.
A squared-error fit cares about the size of moves and not about how many trades win, so this share only describes the trades the calibrated score happened to produce.
The hard call cuts the curve at one half, so it tests the sign of the best-subset fit together with the intercept that the validation rows chose.
Averaging the hit rate over up bars and down bars shows whether the few selected signals separate the two sides or the curve's intercept simply favours one.
One symmetric number for the four outcomes of the incumbent subset's calls, convenient for comparing folds of this same model as the up share of the bars changes.

The search minimised squared error and no likelihood, so this proper score grades the pair of the least-squares score and the logistic curve fitted on validation, read against quoting the fold's training up share.
A bounded proper score of the same score-plus-curve pair, less dominated than the logarithmic loss by a few bars where the selected signals pointed confidently the wrong way.
The curve was fitted without class weights, so its odds are meant to match frequencies, and this checks whether the slope and intercept found on validation rows still hold on test bars.
It gives in points how far the rescaled best-subset fit lands from the realised move, read beside the no-change forecast's error on the same resolved bars.
A least-squares subset is chosen to co-move with the forward move, so the correlation of forecast and realised move on test bars is the fitted relationship checked where it was not fitted.
The forecast is a positive or negative multiple of the same score that feeds the curve, so its sign accuracy shows what the direction call would be without the validation-fitted intercept.
A share of up calls near zero or one means the curve's intercept outweighs the small best-subset score, which turns the trading numbers into a constant-position result.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: The training channel is a residual sum of squares and the validation channel is a logarithmic loss, two different quantities whose difference means nothing.
The engine holds a position on every bar once the curve gives a probability, so exposure describes the engine's rule and not the subset search.
This is the outer tuning score shared by every model and is unrelated to the residual sum of squares the tree search certified.

caveats: The certificate covers only the training-span least-squares problem: a subset proven best in sample is the most overfit subset of its size and the proof says nothing about later bars.
When the node limit stops the tree before it is exhausted the incumbent is returned with its proven gap to the smallest open bound, and that gap is logged but not stored as a metric.
The validation logarithmic loss drawn after each solver pass comes from a curve refitted on those same validation rows, so it is in sample for the curve's slope and intercept and selects nothing.
The price forecast is the same score times one through-origin slope fitted on the clipped training target, so it is a readout of the direction model and not a second independent model.
Absolute-error skill is reported for a forecast that was fitted by squared error, and forecasts are rounded to the tick before scoring.
Consecutive scored bars share future bars because the label horizon overlaps, so any interval around these numbers needs a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance.
For roots other than the Micro Nasdaq contract the costs are that contract's account figures applied as a stated assumption, and the fold's last bar exits at its close.

greedy_selection.summary: Adds signals one at a time, always the one with the most new edge per unit of risk, and never takes a choice back, until the risk budget or the signal limit is reached.
greedy_selection.implementationNote: Bridge: Ratio greedy adds the signal with the most new IC per unit of risk, never undoing a choice; weights IC/variance. P(up) is a curve fitted on validation. Differs from the spec: It weights this model's causal signals by train-span information coefficients (IC): one instrument alone makes it bang-bang on a sign. No optimality guarantee; the order is logged. Expect: forward-stepwise skill; its value is transparency.

maximum_selected_signals.label: Most signals selected
maximum_selected_signals.description: The largest number of signals the program may give weight to.

risk_budget.label: Risk budget
risk_budget.description: Total risk the chosen signals may carry, counted in units of the average signal's profit-stream deviation (6 = six average signals).

minimum_marginal_gain.label: Smallest marginal gain
minimum_marginal_gain.description: Stops when no remaining signal adds at least this much gain.

native.produces: One forward pass returns the selected subset or sequence of candidates, its total objective value and, where the problem has matroid or submodular structure, the approximation ratio that structure guarantees.
native.targetVariable: the total value of the candidates selected under a feasibility constraint such as a budget, a margin cap or a limit on how many may be chosen
native.objectiveNote: The method adds no search beyond always taking the candidate with the largest marginal gain and never undoing a choice, so its quality rests entirely on the ranking rule and on whether the problem has matroid or submodular structure.

metrics.why: A greedy pass can promise a share of the best achievable value only when the gain function has diminishing returns or the feasible sets form a matroid, and that promise is known before any data is seen, so it is stated as a bound and never as a measurement.
metrics.baseline: one minus one over e for a monotone submodular gain, and no guarantee at all where that structure is absent

metrics.why: Because no choice is ever taken back, a small change in the first ranking can redirect every later pick, so the share of candidates chosen again on the next fold is the direct test of whether the selection is repeatable.
The pass stops when the next candidate no longer fits, so the final selection is checked against the stated budget or cardinality limit to confirm the stopping rule held.

notApplicable.name: Realized Sharpe Ratio
notApplicable.why: The pass outputs a chosen set and its total score, not a return stream, so this ratio grades the ranking scores and the trading rule around the selection and belongs to the as-run layer only.

notApplicable.name: Annualized Alpha
notApplicable.why: Alpha is a benchmark-relative return, while a greedy pass natively reports only which candidates it took and their summed value.

notApplicable.name: Maximum Drawdown
notApplicable.why: A one-pass selection has no equity path through time, so there is no running peak to fall from.

notApplicable.name: Portfolio Turnover
notApplicable.why: Turnover would count how often a traded book changes, and the algorithm itself only ranks and picks candidates once per run.

notApplicable.name: Calmar Ratio
notApplicable.why: Return over drawdown belongs to a strategy that trades the selected set, not to the ranking and picking that produced it.

notApplicable.name: CVaR (99% Tail Risk)
notApplicable.why: Risk can enter as the cost side of the ranking ratio, but the pass does not output a loss distribution whose tail could be measured.

notApplicable.name: Relative optimality gap
notApplicable.why: A single forward pass computes no bound on the best possible selection, so the returned set carries no proven distance from the optimum.

asRun.probabilityNote: The score of a bar is the sum of the selected signals' values times their information-coefficient-over-variance weights, and the probability of up is a two-parameter logistic curve of that score fitted by unweighted maximum likelihood on the fold's validation rows.

meaningful.why: The greedy weights define a continuous score per bar, and this ranking number tests whether the signals picked for their training-span information coefficients still order up bars above down bars, using the fitted curve only through the sign of its slope.

Each signal was ranked by the mean profit of trading it alone on training bars, so net profit of the combined call on the test walk is the nearest out-of-sample reading of what the ranking promised, now with real costs.
The ranking ratio divided new information by profit-stream risk, and this per-bar ratio on the test walk shows whether that in-sample trade-off between edge and variation carried over.
The signals are not re-centred, so a selection of mostly positive columns can amount to staying long, and subtracting the same folds' buy-and-hold result shows what the picks added.
The risk budget limited summed profit-stream deviation on training bars, and the deepest fall of the test equity shows whether that budget contained losses once the picks were traded together.
It sets summed winning trades against summed losing trades from the selected signals' combined call, describing how the net result was built and not a quantity the pass ranked on.
The information coefficient is a mean profit that weighs big moves more than small ones, so the share of winning trades only describes the trades the combined score produced.
The hard call cuts the curve at one half, so it tests the sign of the greedy score together with the intercept that the validation rows chose.
Averaging the hit rate over up bars and down bars shows whether the handful of selected signals separates the two sides or the curve's intercept simply favours one.
One symmetric number for the four outcomes of the selected signals' calls, convenient for comparing folds of this same model as the up share of the bars changes.

The pass maximised marginal gain and no likelihood, so this proper score grades the pair of the greedy score and the logistic curve fitted on validation, read against quoting the fold's training up share.
A bounded proper score of the same score-plus-curve pair, steadier than the logarithmic loss on the few bars where the selected signals agree confidently and are wrong.
The curve was fitted without class weights, so its odds are meant to match frequencies, and this checks whether the slope and intercept found on validation rows still hold on test bars.

The forecast is the greedy score times one slope fitted on the training span, so its skill against the no-change forecast tests whether the size of the combined signal says anything about the size of the move.
It states in points how far the rescaled greedy score lands from the realised move, a readout the selection was never fitted for, beside the no-change forecast's error.
The forecast is a multiple of the same score that feeds the curve, so its sign accuracy shows what the direction call would be without the validation-fitted intercept.
With few signals selected the score can be small on most bars, and a share of up calls near zero or one shows the curve's intercept deciding the call instead of the picks.

The engine holds a position on every bar once the curve gives a probability, so exposure describes the engine's rule and not the selection pass.
This is the outer tuning score shared by every model and is unrelated to the marginal gains the pass ranked on.

The order of selection and the marginal gains are written to the log and the fit diagnostics but are not stored as metrics, so recurrence of the selected set across folds cannot yet be read from the record.
The single validation logarithmic loss drawn for the fit comes from a curve fitted on those same validation rows, so it is in sample for the curve's slope and intercept and selects nothing.
The price forecast is the same score times one through-origin slope fitted on the clipped training target, so it is a readout of the direction model and not a second independent model.

submodular_selection.summary: Picks a small set of signals that together represent all the others (coverage) while favouring the ones with training edge, with a proven guarantee of reaching at least 63% of the best possible set.
submodular_selection.implementationNote: Bridge: Lazy greedy maximises coverage of signal correlations plus weighted relevance (the 1 - 1/e bound is logged); weights sign(IC)/k. P(up) is a curve fitted on validation. Differs from the spec: It weights this model's causal signals by train-span information coefficients (IC): one instrument alone makes it bang-bang on a sign. Skill comes only from the relevance term. Expect: a diverse, equal-weight set, below the QP.

maximum_selected_signals.label: Most signals selected
maximum_selected_signals.description: The largest number of signals the program may give weight to.

relevance_weight.label: Relevance weight
relevance_weight.description: How much a signal's own training edge counts against how well it covers the other signals.

native.produces: Submodular optimisation returns a chosen subset of at most a budgeted number of candidates, the value of the diminishing-returns set function on that subset, and the a-priori guarantee that this value is at least one minus one over e of the best possible subset's value.
native.targetVariable: Which candidates (instruments, features or signals) belong to the budgeted subset that maximises a coverage, diversity or representativeness score with diminishing returns
native.objectiveNote: What the diminishing-returns property adds to plain greedy picking is twofold: a proven floor on how good the picked set is, and the lazy shortcut in which a candidate's old marginal gain is an upper bound on its current one and need not be recomputed.

metrics.why: For a set function that never decreases and has diminishing returns, picking the largest marginal gain each time is proven to reach one minus one over e of the best subset's value, and that floor, known before any data is seen, is the whole certificate this method offers.
metrics.baseline: The mathematical constant one minus one over e, which is the floor and not a measurement of this run

metrics.why: The coverage score is built from trailing correlations between candidates, so when those correlations drift the picked subset can change wholesale, and the share of refits in which each candidate is picked again tells whether the subset is a finding or an accident of one window.
metrics.baseline: The share expected if the same number of candidates were drawn at random from the ground set on every refit

metrics.why: The guarantee is stated for a cardinality limit, so the picked subset must hold no more candidates than the selection budget, and a residual above zero would void the floor.
metrics.baseline: A residual of zero, where the subset size does not exceed the budget

metrics.why: Plotting the set function's value after each pick shows the diminishing returns directly, and the pick at which the curve flattens is the specification's own guide for how large the selection budget needs to be.
metrics.baseline: The value of the empty set, which is zero

metrics.why: The lazy priority queue recomputes a candidate's marginal gain only when it reaches the top, so the number of gain evaluations against the budget times the ground-set size that plain greedy would need measures what the shortcut saved.
metrics.baseline: The evaluations plain greedy needs on the same ground set, which is the budget times the number of candidates

notApplicable.name: Realized Sharpe Ratio
notApplicable.why: It measures the engine's trading of a call built from the picked subset and is reported as run, not as the selection's own score.

notApplicable.name: Annualized Alpha
notApplicable.why: A subset chosen for coverage has no return stream and no benchmark, so alpha is undefined for it.

notApplicable.name: Maximum Drawdown
notApplicable.why: It is a traded-equity path statistic that exists only as run, while the selection outputs a set and its value.

notApplicable.name: Portfolio Turnover
notApplicable.why: The engine's turnover is an as-run measure, and the native question of how much the subset changes is answered by the structure stability share.

notApplicable.name: Calmar Ratio
notApplicable.why: Both of its parts are traded quantities that a greedy subset selection never produces by itself.

notApplicable.name: CVaR (99% Tail Risk)
notApplicable.why: The generator stamped a portfolio tail-risk measure on a method whose output is a subset with a coverage score.

notApplicable.name: Relative optimality gap
notApplicable.why: Greedy picking proves no bound on the particular subset it returns beyond the a-priori floor, so there is no measured gap between this answer and the best one.

notApplicable.name: Logarithmic loss
notApplicable.why: The method selects a subset and learns no weights and no probability, so natively there are no stated odds to score.

asRun.standInNote: The specification is a subset selector with no predictor; the runnable adapter treats each feature column of this one instrument as a signal, lets lazy greedy pick the columns that best cover the others' correlations plus a relevance term from each column's training-span information coefficient, gives every picked column an equal weight carrying the sign of its information coefficient, and reads the summed score through a validation-fitted curve, so every as-run number measures that equal-weight signed score plus its readout and not the quality of the selection.
asRun.probabilityNote: The probability of up is a logistic curve, with slope and intercept fitted by unweighted maximum likelihood on the validation rows, applied to the equal-weight signed sum of the picked feature columns for the bar.

stepQuantity.unit: minus the coverage-plus-relevance set value on training rows, and nats per scored bar on validation rows

meaningful.why: The picked columns vote with equal weight and the sign of their training-span information coefficient, and net profit on the walked test bars is what following the sign of that vote, as rescaled by the curve, earned after costs.
The equal-weight signed sum is a continuous score, and this tests whether bars with a higher sum went up more often, which depends only on the picked set and its signs and not on the curve's scale.
The curve's intercept can turn the signed sum into a standing long lean, so the profit left after subtracting buy and hold shows whether the picked columns added a decision.
It restates the profit of the equal-weight vote's direction calls per unit of bar-to-bar swing, with zero only an arithmetic marker because a vote with no skill still pays costs.
The set function rewards coverage and relevance and never looks at an equity path, so the deepest fall of test equity is a risk the greedy picks did not consider.
It compares the winning with the losing trades produced when the equal-weight vote of the picked columns changes sign.
The share of the vote's closed trades that ended positive, read beside the profit factor because an equal-weight sum of standardised columns flips often.
How often the sign of the curve applied to the equal-weight sum matched the move, where the cut sits at the intercept the validation rows chose and not at a sum of zero.
Averaging the hit rate on up bars and down bars shows whether the picked columns separate the two or the curve's intercept simply leans one way.
One symmetric figure for agreement between the vote's calls and the outcomes, near zero when the only skill available, the relevance term's signs, did not carry over to the test bars.
It grades the odds of the equal-weight sum after the validation-fitted curve, so it tests the picked set and the curve together, since the greedy selection itself states no probability.
A bounded second look at the same curve-shaped odds, less swayed by the few bars where several picked columns are extreme at once.
The curve is fitted without class weights, so its odds are meant to match the base rate, and this shows whether a slope and intercept from the validation rows still fit the test bars.
A bin-free check of whether the scale the validation rows gave the equal-weight sum is too confident on test bars, which happens when the signs learned in training stop holding.

The forecast is the price model's own equal-weight sum of picked columns times one least-squares slope through the origin fitted on training rows, so its skill against the no-change forecast tests a one-number rescaling of the selected set.
The size in points of the miss of that slope-times-sum readout, read beside the no-change forecast's error on the same resolved bars.
How often the sign of the slope-times-sum readout matched the move, which grades the signs given to the picked columns more directly than the curve-cut call does.

The forecast takes its sign from a training-fitted slope and the call from a validation-fitted curve with an intercept, so the share of bars where they agree shows how far the curve moved or inverted the sum.
Shows whether the curve's intercept has turned the equal-weight sum into a call of up on nearly every bar, in which case the trading numbers are close to buy and hold.
Counts the flips of the vote's call, read beside every trading number because cost is charged on each flip.
The search over the number of picked signals and the relevance weight scores each trial on inner blocks of the training span, so the best trial's score is a selection score and reads optimistic.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: The training channel holds the negated set value of the picked columns and the validation channel holds a logarithmic loss, two different quantities whose difference means nothing.
With no flat state the engine holds a position on every bar once the first call is made, so exposure describes the engine's rule and not the selection.

caveats: The coverage part of the set function never reads the outcome, so any skill comes only from the relevance term and from the signs taken from training-span information coefficients.
The guarantee of one minus one over e is about the coverage-plus-relevance set value and says nothing about profit or accuracy.
The validation loss shown for the solver pass comes from a curve fitted on those same validation rows, so it is an in-sample figure for the curve.
The selection is a single greedy pass with nothing chosen on validation, and the curve's slope and intercept are the only parameters that saw validation rows.
If the validation rows give the curve a negative slope, the traded call is the opposite of the sign of the equal-weight sum.
The direction model and the price model each run their own greedy pass on the training rows, and the price forecast is tick-rounded before scoring.
Targets of neighbouring bars overlap by the label horizon, so intervals for these numbers need a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance and never a binomial interval.
For roots other than the Micro Nasdaq contract the costs are that contract's account figures applied as a stated assumption.
The last bar of each fold exits at its close while every other exit fills at the next bar's open.
